reasoning:
I'm working out realistic fennec fox proportions—small body, large ears, proper scale in meters—to inform the 3D model I'll build with the SDK.

Now I'm planning the joint hierarchy for the skeleton: hips as root, then a spine chain running through chest, neck, head, and jaw, with specific coordinates mapped out to match the fox's anatomy and pose facing forward.

Checking weightsOf confirms it falls back to nearestJoint when no weights are built, so a root joint at the same position resolves correctly as parent. I'll simplify by creating a "hips" root joint first, then building the spine chain from it, followed by neck and head joints in sequence.

For the roles, I'll keep joint roles minimal and assign chain-level roles instead — "leg" for legs, "neck" for neck, "head" for the head joint, "tail" for the tail, and leave ears simple rather than giving them a special hinge role. The tail will use a catmull spline through four points curving from the hips backward and slightly upward, producing three spans named tail1 through tail3. For the legs, I'm setting up hip, knee, and ankle joints per side leading into a foot, building each as its own chain.

For legs, I'm working out that a polyline with four points (hip, knee, ankle, toe) gives three spans and four joint names, with the last one being the tip joint at the toe. I plan to sweep each leg chain into a tapered tube, narrowing the radius from the hip toward the foot.

Now I'm mapping out actual coordinates for front legs (shoulder, elbow, wrist, toe) and hind legs (hip, knee, hock, foot), keeping the digitigrade bend where the hock angles back before the foot touches the ground, and making sure the toe sits just above floor level so the rounded cap rests naturally on it. Right legs will just mirror the left by negating the x-coordinate.

For the joint-building function, I'm naming sides with L/R suffixes (hipL, kneeL, etc.) to stay compatible with the naming rules, and considering whether to add paw/toe shapes as small spheres attached to each foot bone versus skipping them for simplicity. For the head, I'm laying out a loft shape — a skull-and-snout profile built from a sequence of stations (nose, muzzle, cheek, skull) each with its own width and height to get that stylized fennec head shape.

Now I'm deciding how to bind the head loft to the skeleton — since the path runs from the back of the neck up to the nose, the nearest-joint default could incorrectly weight it to the neck joint instead of the head. I'm leaning toward just rigidly binding the entire head loft to the "head" joint for simplicity, accepting a less smooth neck transition since this is a puppet-style rig anyway.

For the body I'm planning a loft of stations along the spine from rump to chest, using ellipsoidal widths/heights that taper toward a slim fennec build, and binding it to the spine chain so the skin smoothly follows all the spine joints via Catmull interpolation. Then for the neck I'm setting up a separate sweep along a neck chain connecting the chest to the head joint, tapering the radius down as it approaches the skull.

I'm now working out joint hierarchy and naming so everything parents correctly: the spine chain should start right at the hips root joint, with its spans producing named joints like spine1 and spine2, and the chest position becoming the parent anchor for the neck chain that follows.

But I realize making the chain's own first joint serve as the root fails, since bone resolution requires at least one existing joint to find nearest neighbors — so I need a root joint to exist before the first chain can be built.

So I'll place a "hips" root joint, then build the spine chain starting right at the hips point even though it duplicates the location, which is harmless. For the ears, I'm planning a pointed, upright triangular outline (roughly 15cm tall, 10cm wide at base) that I'll extrude along the side-facing plane to get the fennec-style ear shape.

Working out the ear placement at the top of the head, tilting the outline plane back slightly and adjusting the ear height down to around 0.12 so the proportions relative to body height don't look exaggerated. I'm sketching the ear outline points now, making sure the tip is sharp and the base corners are rounded, checking the winding order is counterclockwise before extruding.

For the ear material, I'm leaning toward tan/sand on the outer side and white on the inner side, and planning the overall fox fur using a countershade paint going from tan on the back to cream on the belly, plus a position-based mask for white cheeks and muzzle on the head.

For the eyes, I'm working out how to place embedded spheres accurately on the head surface using a surface-hit lookup against the loft mesh rather than guessing coordinates manually, so the eyes sit naturally sunk into the skull at the muzzle region.

For the nose, I'm similarly using a surface-nearest hit at the muzzle tip to position a small dark sphere, embedding it slightly so it reads as a snout rather than floating above the skin.

For the ears, I'm deciding to skip separate inner-ear geometry and instead paint color variation directly onto the extruded ear mesh, blending tan and cream tones along its length using the surface paint coordinates.

For the tail, I'm building a Catmull-Rom chain of points tapering from the hips outward with a radius profile that bulges slightly then narrows, and using a z-position check in the paint function so the tip renders white while the rest blends into the body's countershading. I'm naming the tail segments and setting the chain's role, then moving on to start defining the leg chains.

For the legs, I'm laying out polyline chains through shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw joints (four points, three spans) so each joint gets a unique name per side, setting the leg's contact point at the toe, and letting the nearest existing spine joint act as parent for the shoulder joint. Then I'm sweeping each leg chain with a tapering radius array so the limb narrows from shoulder to paw, relying on default rounded caps at both ends since the paw sits exposed at the bottom.

I'm placing a flattened sphere at each toe for the foot pad, using a scale vector to squash it into a paw shape and a pale cream color to match fennec fur, then working out coordinates for front legs (shoulder-elbow-wrist-toe) and hind legs with a digitigrade bend, where the hock angles back before the foot comes forward to the toe point.

Now I'm defining the body as a lofted shape along a spine chain with station widths and heights tapering from rump to chest, catmull-interpolated between keyframe positions, and making sure the loft's color paint is set since sweep requires it even though the chain bone mapping handles joint placement separately from the path geometry.

Working out the neck tube radii and verifying the body/chest cross-section heights line up so the neck sits flush against the torso, then placing the head joint at the top of the neck chain with default parent orientation.

Now I'm adding a lower jaw as its own small loft, with stations tapering from a wider base near the hinge joint down to a narrower tip, bound to a "jaw" bone so it can rotate independently from the head, using the parent's orientation by default since no explicit direction is given.

I'm sketching the ear shape as a leaf-like outline with a sharp tip, computing placement coordinates on either side of the midline, and deciding on a cream-to-tan gradient paint for the fur with simple extrude parameters for thickness and bevel.

For the eyes and nose, I'm computing surface hit points on the head mesh to orient spheres that are slightly scaled for an almond shape, plus a smaller dark sphere for the nose, while deciding to skip whiskers, inner-ear highlights, and a mouth to keep things simple.

I'm considering adding fur tufts using card geometry with a tuft-shaped SVG texture, scattering them on the belly and chest region using surface hit filtering based on normal direction, with a leaning/flow direction to simulate hanging fur, while weighing the complexity and rendering risk this adds.

I'm defining the coat color scheme using a countershade paint between a sandy tan and cream, plus a separate paint function for the white facial mask with a hard boundary for a bold stylized look, and deciding body, legs, and jaw should mostly share the same coat paint while paws and muzzle get the cream tone.

Now I'm structuring the actual import statements and builder calls—setting up loft stations for the head and body with named bones, rigid skinning per joint, and sweep options like segment count for a slightly faceted stylized look, making sure joint creation order respects the hip-to-spine-to-neck-to-head-to-jaw hierarchy before building out the leg chains from the shoulders.

I'm recalculating the overall body proportions since my initial coordinates made the fox too elongated compared to real fennec proportions, rescaling the spine, neck, head, and tail positions to compress the nose-to-rump length and tail length to more realistic figures, and adjusting leg joint heights for a digitigrade stance.

I'm placing sphere-based paw geometry at the end of each leg chain, scaling them to flatten slightly and sit correctly at ground level, then moving to the ear extrusion definitions with a sharp-tipped outline, bevel, and smoothing, plus a gradient paint from cream at the base to tan at the tip.
